rv.q: Wonderful Sutton Foster and thrilling, dirt-kicking musical.
Driven by a performance of incandescent yearning from Sutton Foster that’s all the more moving for its restraint, Violet is a delicate wildflower, craning toward the sun.
But pep-allergic people will not need to steel themselves to see the terrific, heart-stirring revival of 'Violet.'
But the most unlikely thing about Violet is that it makes of these outré elements, these horrible and troubling specificities, a work of great resonance and beauty and joy.
Let’s hope so, because helmer Leigh Silverman and collaborating creatives have done a lovely job of reviving this winsome 1997 musical by Brian Crawley (book & lyrics) and Jeanine Tesori (music).
Though flawed on its face, Violet provides—as Flick sings in the show’s best song—reason to rejoice.
In these all-important moments, the storytelling becomes muddied and you don't get the emotional payoff I've seen with this piece before.
And with Sutton Foster in the title role, its Broadway premiere is an absolute triumph that should not be missed.
And what a wonderful trip it is.
You’ll feel as though you’re witnessing a star being reborn, 18 years into her career.

It’s impossible not to get swept up by rousing numbers like Violet’s ”On My Way” and Flick’s ”Let It Sing” (Henry pretty much blows the roof off the bus with that one) — or to resist Foster’s pluck and aw-shucks charm.
It turns out to be a superior musical.

But Silverman and her cast reward our patience with performances that transcend clichés, taking care to make the fragility of these characters, and their different quests for dignity and love, authentic.
The generic hillbilly twang that everyone sports is just make believe.

The moment Violet encounters the evangelist, who's with his choir, you know the singers will perform a rousing hallelujah number ("Raise Me Up"), led by an African-American woman (Rema Webb). The takeaway from the show, after Violet finds love but not physical transformation, is that true beauty lies within.
Sutton Foster, a two-time Tony winner, gives her most expressive, deeply felt and vibrant performance to date, fully capturing the character's yearning and volatility.
As Violet – the woman with a dream to shoot out of her life and into a new world
Foster proves she can do anything with her brilliantly grounded yet soaring performance in Violet.
